questions.question: Q: What are DRVs and why are they important?

points.text: Dietary Reference Values are estimates of nutrient requirements for different population groups. RNI (Reference Nutrient Intake) is the amount sufficient for almost all individuals. EAR (Estimated Average Requirement) meets the needs of 50% of the population. LRNI is the intake below which deficiency is likely. DRVs help plan diets, formulate policy, and assess population nutritional status.

questions.question: Q: Evaluate how well the UK population follows the Eatwell Guide.

points.text: Most UK diets deviate significantly from the Eatwell Guide: too much saturated fat, sugar, and salt; too little fibre, fruit, vegetables, and oily fish. Only about 30% of adults eat 5-a-day. Processed foods high in fat, sugar, and salt make up a large proportion of energy intake. markScheme.exemplarAnswer: A nutritionally balanced day for a 15-year-old vegetarian girl must meet increased needs for iron, calcium, and protein during adolescence while addressing the limitations of a vegetarian diet. Breakfast: Porridge made with fortified plant milk, topped with berries and seeds. Porridge provides slow-release energy from complex carbohydrates. Fortified plant milk supplies calcium and vitamin D. Berries provide vitamin C (which enhances iron absorption). Seeds add omega-3 fatty acids. Lunch: Wholegrain pitta with hummus, roasted vegetables, and a side salad. The wholegrain pitta provides fibre and B vitamins. Hummus provides protein and iron from chickpeas. The salad vegetables add vitamins and fibre. Adding a glass of orange juice enhances iron absorption from the plant-based meal. Dinner: Tofu stir-fry with mixed vegetables and brown rice. Tofu provides HBV protein and calcium (if set with calcium salts). Mixed vegetables provide a range of vitamins and minerals. Brown rice adds fibre and B vitamins. Using a small amount of sesame oil provides unsaturated fat. Snack: Greek yoghurt (or fortified alternative) with walnuts. This provides calcium, protein, and omega-3 fatty acids. Key nutritional considerations: iron from plant sources (non-haem) is enhanced by vitamin C at each meal; calcium is obtained from fortified products; B12 (only found naturally in animal products) must be obtained from fortified foods or supplements; protein is achieved through complementary combinations
